Basic Principles of Dairy
 Nutrition and Feeding
     Management
         Dr. Walter Chen

Why is Important?
• Proper nutrition and feeding management are critical to
  maintaining health, productivity and reproductive efficiency
• Feed cost represent 60-70% of the total costs
• Improve nutrition and feeding management increase
  production and feed efficiency

Nutritional Requirements
• Dairy cows’ diets much be balanced to meet their needs for
  maintenance, lactation, reproduction, and growth.
• Order of priority of meeting nutritional requirements
  • Maintenance
  • Lactation
  • Growth
  • Reproduction

Key Nutrients
• The key nutrients include:
  • Energy
  • Protein
  • Fiber
  • Vitamins and Minerals
  • Water

Energy
• Provided by carbohydrates and fats to support milk
  production
• Starch is the primary source of energy, supplying over 60%
  of the energy
• Grains such as corn, barley is the common source of starch.
• Type of grains and processing method affects starch
  digestibility

Protein
• Needed for milk synthesis and body maintenance
• Source include soybean meal, canola meal, Distiller Dried Grains
  (DDGS) and alfalfa hay
• Protein is further classified as ruminal degradable protein (RDP)
  and ruminal undegradable protein (RUP or commonly called
  rumen bypass protein).
• RDP provides nitrogen for rumen microbial fermentation while
  RUP bypass rumen to be digested and absorbed in the intestine.
• Dairy cows’ diet must be balanced for RDP and RUP
• Amino acid balance is also very important consideration when
  formulating dairy cow ration.

Fiber
• Is essential for proper rumen function
• Found in hay and silage

Vitamins and Minerals
• Macro minerals: Calcium, Phosphorus, Magnesium,
  Potassium, Salt, Sulfur
• Microminerals: Zn, Mn, Se, Co, I, Cu
• Vitamins: A, D & E

Water
• Water consumption is 2-4
  times of milk production
• As temperature raises,
  water consumption
  increases 1-2 folds.
• Drinking plenty water helps
    • Cool cows down
    • Reduce risk of rumen
      acidosis

Balancing Diets for
Lactating Cows
• Select high quality feed ingredients
• Provide adequate effective fiber
• Balance for rumen degradable starch
  and rumen degradable protein to
  maximize rumen microbial fermentation

(DDGS) is a by-product of corn
processing to produce ethanol.
•During the production process, the
starch fermentation in corn is
converted into ethanol, which is
extracted by distillation, and the
remaining products are proteins,
fats, fibers and ash.

Benefits of Feeding DDGS
• High protein content- 30% commonly used to replace
  soybean meal, canola meal and other source of protein
• High rumen bypass protein -50% of CP
• High energy content – 2-2.2 Macal/kg
• Digestible fiber –can replace some forage such as corn
  silage or alfalfa hay
• Can be fed up to 20% of the diet DM depending on the
  ration

Use of Total Mixed
Ration in Dairy Cows
• Total Mixed Ration or TMR mixes all ingredients
  such as forage, grains, minerals and vitamins
  together to provide a consistent ration
• Each bite should have balanced nutrients
• Better rumen health
• Increase dry matter intake and feed efficiency

Feed Bunk
Management
• Provide minimum 60cm feeding space per
  cow
• Allow cows to access to feed 20 hour a day
• Manage feed amount to reduce feed
  refusal to 2-5%
• Remove feed refusal every day
• Increase feeding frequency to 2-3 time a
  day
• Push up feed frequently (6-8 times a day)
• Do not lock cows up in the feed bunk
